title: Capstone A: the night shift
summary: Run an overnight shift alone for an accounting firm in Brisbane: an unlabelled, noisy queue of twelve alerts, one real intrusion hiding in it, and a morning team waiting for your escalation, a new detection and a shift report.
rubric: Queue: all twelve alerts have a disposition and a reason backed by a log line
Scope: the one affected host, user, tool and destination named, with the evidence
Escalation: the ask first, severity with its reason, know / don't know, evidence location
New detection: a Sigma rule that catches the renamed copy tool before data moves, tested, with a tuning note
Shift report: open items by ID with owners, closed items, watch list, calls with times
Hints: minus 1 point for each hint opened (write the count in the shift report)
Working alone: every search and command kept in the notebook
handin: A shift report, one escalation and one new detection rule, plus the dispositioned queue.

script.intro: This is Capstone A, the night shift. You work for a managed SOC, a company that watches other companies' networks around the clock. Tonight's client is Wattle and Finch Accountants, a fourteen-person practice in Brisbane. When it's ten in the morning in Brisbane, it's half past five in India, so their working day is your night. The queue has twelve alerts and no severities, because the client's old SIEM doesn't send them. One real intrusion is hiding in there. In a capstone the steps tell you what to deliver, not how, and every hint you open costs a point. I'll walk the whole shift once, so you can see what good looks like, and then it's your turn.

steps.say: Step one: how the night desk works. A capstone uses every program from seminars two and three at once, so start by seeing how they fit. The alert queue says what you have to decide. The SIEM says how big it is: which hosts, how often, how much data. The event viewer says exactly what ran on one laptop and what started it. The packet viewer shows what really crossed the wire. The intel feed and ATT&CK say whether anyone has seen this before and what to call it. Sigma leaves a better rule behind. And the report builder turns it all into words for the client. Let's see what the SIEM can search tonight.
steps.after: Eight sources and 308 events. The biggest is dns.log, with 148 queries from every laptop in the office, then the firewall's session log, with 62 connections. Those two cover the whole office. The three Windows event logs and the process list come from one laptop only, acc-lt03, which tells you that someone has already pulled extra evidence from it. The alert queue and the intel feed are JSON, so the SIEM reads them too. The packet capture isn't here at all: the packet viewer reads it. Notice what this firm doesn't have: a web proxy. Laptops go straight out through the firewall, so the firewall's log is the only record of where the data went. Answer the question: dns.log.

steps.say: Step two: start of shift. Before touching anything, hash the evidence and read the queue end to end. Twelve alerts. Write down your first guess of which ones belong together, because we'll test it.
steps.after: Twelve alerts, and one host keeps coming up: acc-lt03, the practice manager's laptop. A download at 00:03, a remote access tool at 00:04, discovery commands at 00:09, a program written to ProgramData at 00:13 and a large upload at 00:46. The rest are spread across the office: an inbox rule, Windows Update, failed logons, an archive job, a new service, a new phone, and an unknown device on the Wi-Fi. That's my first guess: one intrusion on acc-lt03, and a lot of ordinary Thursday morning. Answer the question: twelve.

steps.say: Step three: work the queue. Every alert gets a disposition and a reason that points at evidence. Severity is yours to judge. And the five alerts that belong to one intrusion should say so, so the client reads one story, not five.
steps.after: The five on acc-lt03 are escalated together: AL-8401, 8403, 8404, 8408 and 8406. Now the noise, and every one of these has a reason. AL-8402, a new inbox rule, sounds alarming, because attackers love inbox rules for hiding replies. But this one moves tax-office letters into a folder called Tax Office, and it was made in Outlook on a.nguyen's own laptop from the office's own internet address. Benign. AL-8405 is Windows Update during the patch push. AL-8407 is four typing mistakes with Caps Lock on, then a good logon from the same desk. AL-8409 is the monthly archive job, and AL-8410 a service installed during the patch window, both under change numbers. AL-8411 is a new iPhone, with MFA approved, from the office. And AL-8412, an unknown Android device on the staff Wi-Fi, gets needs more information, with a question for the office manager: did someone connect a new phone today? Answer the question: acc-lt03.

steps.say: Step four: scope it with search. Before you escalate, know how big it is. Which laptop sent the most data out? Where did it go, and does anyone else send data there? Who else talked to the fake support site? And what did the firewall stop? We finish by writing the cloud storage search again in KQL, to check ourselves.
steps.after: acc-lt03 sent about 2.26 gigabytes out of the office. The next highest, reception, sent about five megabytes. Everyone else sent less than one. Now storage.cloudbox.example: two hosts. Reception sent two small uploads, three and a half megabytes and just over one megabyte, which fits the intel file: reception uses that cloud storage to send files to clients. acc-lt03 sent eight uploads of around 270 megabytes each. Same site, very different story. And that's the hard lesson of tonight: the data went to a site that's on the allow list. Only one client ever asked DNS for ledgerpro-support.example: 10.40.0.23, acc-lt03. And the firewall denied two things: acc-lt01 trying an outside time server, which is policy noise, and acc-lt03 trying filedrop.example, an anonymous file-sharing site, at 00:15. The KQL version gives the same two hosts. Answer the questions: acc-lt03, two, and filedrop.example.

steps.say: Step five: confirm on the host and the wire. Search results are a summary, so now we confirm on the laptop's own logs and in the packet capture. Sysmon event 1 records every program that starts, with its command line, its parent, and one more field that matters a lot tonight: OriginalFileName, the name the program was built with. Renaming the file doesn't change it.
steps.after: Seventeen programs started. Follow the chain. At 00:02 Chrome opened the firm's real accounting software, app.ledgerpro.example. At 00:03 it went to ledgerpro-support.example instead, a lookalike, and at 00:04 LedgerPro_Support.exe was saved and run. Its OriginalFileName is RemoteHelper.exe: it's a remote access tool. It installed a service, started an agent, and connected to relay.remotehelper.example. From 00:09, through that agent, someone ran whoami, then net use, which lists the network drives, and then counted the PDFs in S Clients 2026, the client files on the file server. At 00:12 PowerShell downloaded a zip from a software mirror, and at 00:13 svc-sync.exe appeared in ProgramData. Filter for rclone.exe and three events match: svc-sync.exe is rclone, a free tool for copying files to cloud storage, run once to test it, once towards filedrop, which the firewall blocked, and at 00:16 towards cloudbox, with eight transfers at once. Network events show eight connections to 203.0.113.150. And in the capture, the filter on the TLS server name shows eight Client Hellos to storage.cloudbox.example: the start of eight upload streams. Answer the questions: relay.remotehelper.example, svc-sync.exe, rclone.exe, 00:16, and 203.0.113.150.

steps.say: Step six: check the indicators. Pull every indicator out of the evidence and check it against the intel feed and the client's allow list. Then map the behaviour to ATT&CK, so the morning team, the client and anyone they report to use the same words.
steps.after: ledgerpro-support.example is on the vendor feed as malicious: a phone scam where callers pretend to be accounting-software support, first seen on the ninth of November. So the most likely story is a phone call. j.walsh was talked into downloading a support tool. The remote-access relay is suspicious because this client doesn't use any remote access tool. The software mirror and filedrop are suspicious by category. And storage.cloudbox.example is on the client's own allow list. You can't simply block it without breaking reception's work, which is why the detection has to be about behaviour, not destination. On the heatmap: spearphishing by voice, remote access software, the three discovery techniques, ingress tool transfer for the download, masquerading for the renamed rclone, and exfiltration to cloud storage. Defang everything before it leaves your notebook. Answer the question: ledgerpro-support.example.

steps.say: Step seven: escalate. One escalation for the whole intrusion, not one per alert. The reader is the practice principal, reading on a phone between client meetings. The ask goes first, with a time in UTC and in Brisbane time. Then severity and the fact that decided it, what we know, what we don't, and what we have and haven't changed.
steps.after: The ask: approve isolating acc-lt03 now, by 01:30 UTC, half past eleven in Brisbane, ask j.walsh to stop using it, and ask her who phoned her this morning. Severity high, and the deciding fact is in one sentence: about 2.2 gigabytes of client tax files have already left, and someone outside has remote control of the laptop right now. Then the timeline, each line with its alert and its file. What we don't know: exactly which files, whether the copy has finished, and whether she gave the caller a password too. The impact says what was copied, the 2026 tax files of the firm's clients, because that's personal and financial information, and the client may have to tell people. And we say clearly: nothing has been changed on the laptop. The client decides; we give them what they need to decide.

steps.say: Step eight: leave a new detection behind. The client's upload rule, AL-8406, fired at 00:46, half an hour after the copy started, because it waits until a gigabyte has gone. We want a rule that fires before any data moves. Something the copy tool did that normal programs don't do. We write it in Sigma, test it, and write what would make it noisy.
steps.after: The rule: a Sysmon process event where OriginalFileName is rclone.exe, but the file isn't called rclone.exe. A program built as rclone and running under another name is hiding. It matches three events, all svc-sync.exe, and nothing else on the laptop. The first match is the test run at 00:14:02. AL-8406 fired at 00:46:10. That's thirty-two minutes earlier, and two minutes before the copy started. The tuning note: some IT tools bundle rclone under their own name, so list those by path and signer if the client ever uses one, and watch the first week of hits in test mode. Answer the questions: three, and thirty-two.

steps.say: Step nine: shift report. Close your shift so that the morning team can carry on without calling you. Everything open, by ID, with an owner. Everything closed, in one line each. What to watch. Who you called, and when. And how many hints you opened.
steps.after: Two items stay open. The incident, with all five alert IDs and the next steps: the client isolates the laptop, and the morning analyst lists exactly which files were copied and helps the client decide who must be told. And the unknown Android device, with its question and an owner. Six alerts are closed, one line each, each with the fact that closed it. The watch list has the three bad domains, any RemoteHelper service, and the new rule in test mode. The calls have times: the practice principal at 01:18, isolation approved at 01:24, and the message to the morning lead. And the hints line, honestly.

steps.say: Step ten: hand in. The notebook carries the queue, the searches, the escalation, the rule and the shift report. The rubric is on screen, including the line that takes a point for each hint.
steps.after: Now it's your turn. Do it at the Practice level first, then Solo, alone, with your hints counted. Read your escalation one last time as the practice principal, on a phone, with a client waiting. If it doesn't tell her what to do in its first two lines, fix that before you hand in.

script.outro: That's the night shift. Twelve alerts with no severities, and one real intrusion: a phone call, a fake support site, a remote access tool, three discovery commands, a renamed copy tool, and two gigabytes of clients' tax files sent to a cloud storage site the firm itself allows. You scoped it with search, confirmed it on the laptop and on the wire, saw why blocking a destination wasn't enough, escalated once with the ask first, and left behind a rule that would have fired thirty-two minutes earlier, before any data moved. That's the whole SOC kit from seminars two and three, used alone, at night, for someone else's company. Next, in seminar five, Incident response, we follow an attack all the way from the first call to the boardroom. Thank you for watching.

# Capstone A: the night shift

Run an overnight shift alone for an accounting firm in Brisbane: an unlabelled, noisy queue of twelve alerts, one real intrusion hiding in it, and a morning team waiting for your escalation, a new detection and a shift report.

The files for this seminar are in `~/case` (Linux) and `case/` (Python): `alerts-night.json`, `capture.pcap`, `dns.log`, `eventlogs/Security.jsonl`, `eventlogs/Sysmon.jsonl`, `eventlogs/System.jsonl`, `fw_sessions.csv`, `intel.json`, `process.csv`, `README.txt`.

## 1. How the night desk works

A capstone uses every program from seminars 2 and 3 at once, so start by seeing how they fit. Each program answers one kind of question, and a night shift moves through them in order:

| Program | The question it answers | Reads |
|---|---|---|
| Alert queue | What do I have to decide tonight? | alerts-night.json |
| SIEM search | How big is it: which hosts, how often, how much data? | fw_sessions.csv, dns.log, process.csv, the event logs |
| Event viewer | What exactly ran on the laptop, started by what? | eventlogs/*.jsonl |
| Packet viewer | What really crossed the wire, and to where? | capture.pcap |
| Indicators and ATT&CK | Has anyone seen this before, and what do we call it? | intel.json |
| Sigma rules | How do we catch it sooner next time? | the event logs |
| Report builder | What does the client need to decide, and what does the morning shift need to know? | your notes |

The client tonight is **Wattle & Finch Accountants** in Brisbane. Their working day is your night. Read `README.txt` first, then run the inventory search below: it shows which files the SIEM can search and how many events each holds. The alert queue and the intel feed are JSON, so the SIEM reads them too. The packet capture isn't in the SIEM; the packet viewer reads it.

- [ ] Run the inventory search
- [ ] Which file holds the most events? Which one is about the whole office, and which only about one laptop?
- [ ] Note which program you would open for each kind of question


```tool siem
{"q": "", "n": 8, "files": ["fw_sessions.csv", "dns.log", "process.csv", "eventlogs/Sysmon.jsonl", "eventlogs/Security.jsonl", "eventlogs/System.jsonl"], "blank": ["q"], "a": {"q": "* | stats count by source sourcetype"}}
```

?> Which evidence file holds the most events? :: sha256:389616bb3f05f22f67c324c1da02da6bbb02f7792854469c24dfb3bab4474c03

## 2. Start of shift

You are the overnight analyst at a managed SOC. The queue has **twelve alerts and no severities**: the client's old SIEM doesn't send them. One real intrusion is in there. The rest is ordinary noise.

This is a capstone: the steps say what to deliver, not how. **Hints cost one point each** on the rubric, so open one only when you are stuck, and write down how many you opened.

Start by hashing the evidence and reading the queue end to end before you touch anything.

- [ ] Hash every evidence file and keep the list
- [ ] Read all twelve alerts once, quickly
- [ ] Write down your first guess of which ones belong together: you will test it


?> How many alerts are in the night queue? :: sha256:6b51d431df5d7f141cbececcf79edf3dd861c3b4069f0b11661a3eefacbba918
# Your turn. Write the code for this step, then press Run.
template.a:
cd ~/case
sha256sum *.* eventlogs/*
echo ---
grep -c '"id"' alerts-night.json
grep -E '"(id|host|rule)"' alerts-night.json

## 3. Work the queue

Give every alert a disposition and a reason. A reason is a log line or a fact you checked, not a feeling. Severity is yours to judge: the queue doesn't tell you.

- [ ] Every alert has a disposition
- [ ] Every reason points at evidence
- [ ] Alerts that belong to one intrusion say so
- [ ] Use "needs more information" only with a question someone can answer


```tool alerts
{"file": "alerts-night.json", "d": "", "n": 5, "blank": ["d"], "a": {"d": {"AL-8401": "escalate", "AL-8402": "benign", "AL-8403": "escalate", "AL-8404": "escalate", "AL-8405": "benign", "AL-8406": "escalate", "AL-8407": "benign", "AL-8408": "escalate", "AL-8409": "benign", "AL-8410": "benign", "AL-8411": "benign", "AL-8412": "more"}}}
```

?> Which host do the related alerts share? :: sha256:7006306a1e36f893caf6a9147da511e6d6f864ecf30bcfd51d8b07cd29285ba5

## 4. Scope it with search

Before you escalate, know how big it is. Which laptop sent the most data out, where did it go, did anyone else talk to the same places, and what did the firewall stop?

- [ ] Which host sent the most bytes out? Is that normal for it?
- [ ] Who sends data to storage.cloudbox.example, and how much? (check intel.json: is that site allowed?)
- [ ] Who else asked DNS for ledgerpro-support.example?
- [ ] What did the firewall deny?
- [ ] Write the cloud-storage search in KQL


```tool siem
{"q": "", "n": 6, "files": ["fw_sessions.csv"], "blank": ["q"], "a": {"q": "source=*fw_sessions.csv | stats sum(bytes_out) as sent by src_host | sort - sent"}}
```

```tool siem
{"q": "", "n": 2, "files": ["fw_sessions.csv"], "blank": ["q"], "a": {"q": "source=*fw_sessions.csv dst_host=storage.cloudbox.example | stats count sum(bytes_out) as sent by src_host"}}
```

```tool siem
{"q": "", "n": 1, "files": ["dns.log"], "blank": ["q"], "a": {"q": "source=*dns.log ledgerpro-support.example | stats count by src_ip"}}
```

```tool siem
{"q": "", "n": 2, "files": ["fw_sessions.csv"], "blank": ["q"], "a": {"q": "source=*fw_sessions.csv action=deny | table _time src_host dst_host dport app"}}
```

```tool siem
{"q": "", "lang": "kql", "n": 2, "files": ["fw_sessions.csv"], "blank": ["q"], "a": {"q": "fw_sessions | where dst_host == \"storage.cloudbox.example\" | summarize sum(bytes_out) by src_host"}}
```

?> Which host sent the most data out? :: sha256:7006306a1e36f893caf6a9147da511e6d6f864ecf30bcfd51d8b07cd29285ba5
?> How many hosts sent data to storage.cloudbox.example? :: sha256:d4735e3a265e16eee03f59718b9b5d03019c07d8b6c51f90da3a666eec13ab35
?> Which site did the firewall block for acc-lt03? :: sha256:4907c3569357f30a966c09a74b595259cb8cff54b2994185944fa02f30aef176

## 5. Confirm on the host and the wire

Search results are a summary. Confirm on the laptop's own logs and on the packet capture: which programs ran, which one sent the data, what it really is, and where the data went.

- [ ] Sysmon event 1: follow the chain from the download to the copy tool
- [ ] Sysmon event 1 shows OriginalFileName, the name the program was built with. Which program is hiding under a new name?
- [ ] Sysmon event 3: which program connected to 203.0.113.150, and how many times?
- [ ] Capture: find the TLS Client Hellos to the storage site


```tool events
{"file": "eventlogs/Sysmon.jsonl", "ids": "", "n": 17, "blank": ["ids", "src", "q"], "a": {"ids": "1"}}
```

```tool events
{"file": "eventlogs/Sysmon.jsonl", "ids": "", "q": "", "n": 3, "blank": ["ids", "src", "q"], "a": {"ids": "1", "q": "rclone.exe"}}
```

```tool events
{"file": "eventlogs/Sysmon.jsonl", "ids": "", "q": "", "n": 8, "blank": ["ids", "src", "q"], "a": {"ids": "3", "q": "203.0.113.150"}}
```

```tool packets
{"file": "capture.pcap", "f": "", "n": 8, "blank": ["f"], "a": {"f": "tls.handshake.extensions_server_name contains cloudbox"}}
```

?> Which domain did the remote access tool connect to? :: sha256:30a80820053d3b0b7c245df61b45c1cca4c778fea876a09584283525046c57c0
?> What file name does the copy tool run under? :: sha256:ffc53d6ac58004e850e60bf30ab4c7fee651a25fd28be01932ca8959f9cb37a0
?> What is its real program name (OriginalFileName)? :: sha256:d5604ae4cfd963fe62b19e369874996d85e77bff20120e7b4d86c2d374caadcd
?> At what time (HH:MM) did the copy that worked start? :: sha256:5bb60732d06083e80e0c4e5c70219c0946c73e0d6b89cc8272e60c7015eff2c8
?> Which IP address received the data? :: sha256:992c86091ff8bac9b6fe49bd09a7fc9be514d3625aafcb290922153132ec0e6b

## 6. Check the indicators

Pull every indicator out of the evidence and check it against the intel feed and the client's allow list. Map what you saw to ATT&CK so the morning team and the client speak the same language.

- [ ] Extract indicators from the logs
- [ ] Which are on the feed, which are new, and which are on the allow list?
- [ ] An allowed destination received the stolen files. What does that mean for blocking?
- [ ] Map the behaviour to ATT&CK techniques
- [ ] Defang indicators before you paste them anywhere


```tool ioc
{"attack": "", "blank": ["iocs", "attack"], "a": {"attack": ["T1566.004", "T1219", "T1033", "T1135", "T1083", "T1105", "T1036", "T1567.002"]}}
```

?> From which domain was the remote access program downloaded? :: sha256:75ac3e11ebbdb1c4fb575107d8fea2e979b89e2934cdde5d6156b73315d55f8b

## 7. Escalate

Write one escalation for the whole intrusion, not one per alert. The client's practice principal reads it on a phone, between clients.

- [ ] The ask first, with a time in UTC and in Brisbane time
- [ ] Severity and the fact that decided it
- [ ] Know / don't know
- [ ] What you have and haven't changed


```tool report
{"tpl": "escalation", "title": "Escalation: client files leaving acc-lt03 through a remote access tool", "text": "", "n": 7, "blank": ["text"], "a": {"text": "# Escalation: client files leaving acc-lt03 through a remote access tool

## The ask

Please approve isolating acc-lt03 (10.40.0.23) from the network now, by 01:30 UTC (11:30 Brisbane), and ask j.walsh to stop using it. Practice principal, please call the SOC on the bridge; please also ask j.walsh who phoned her this morning.

## Severity and why

High: about 2.2 GB of client tax files have already been uploaded to a cloud storage account the firm doesn't own, and someone outside has remote control of the laptop right now.

## What we know

- 00:03 UTC: j.walsh downloaded LedgerPro_Support.exe from ledgerpro-support.example, a domain registered three days ago that copies the name of the firm's real accounting software (AL-8401, fw_sessions.csv, dns.log).
- 00:04 UTC: it is a remote access tool (RemoteHelper). It installed a service and connected to relay.remotehelper.example (AL-8403, System 7045, Sysmon).
- 00:09 to 00:10 UTC: through the remote session, someone ran whoami, net use and a count of PDFs on S:\Clients\2026 (AL-8404).
- 00:12 to 00:14 UTC: PowerShell downloaded a zip from downloads.toolmirror.example and unpacked svc-sync.exe into C:\ProgramData\Sync. Its real name is rclone.exe, a cloud copy tool (AL-8408, Sysmon event 1).
- 00:15 UTC: an upload to filedrop.example was blocked by the firewall.
- 00:16 UTC onwards: svc-sync.exe copied S:\Clients\2026 to storage.cloudbox.example (203.0.113.150) over 8 connections, about 2.2 GB (AL-8406, fw_sessions.csv, capture.pcap).

## What we don't know

- Exactly which client files were copied, and whether the copy has finished.
- Who phoned j.walsh, and whether she gave them a password as well.
- Whether the cloud storage account (wf-bkp-1112) can be reported to the storage provider for removal.

## Impact so far

One laptop, acc-lt03, and one user, j.walsh. The copied folder holds 2026 tax files for the firm's clients: personal and financial information. Only acc-lt03 contacted the fake support site. Reception's normal uploads to the same storage site are small and expected.

## What I've done

Nothing has been changed on the laptop. I have added ledgerpro-support.example, relay.remotehelper.example and downloads.toolmirror.example to the SIEM watch list.

## Evidence

alerts-night.json, fw_sessions.csv, dns.log, process.csv, the three event logs and capture.pcap are saved in the shift folder with SHA-256 hashes.
"}}
```

## 8. Leave a new detection behind

The client's upload rule (AL-8406) fired at 00:46, thirty minutes after the copy started, because it waits for 1 GB. Write a better one: something the copy tool did **before** any data moved, that normal programs don't do. Test it, and write what would make it noisy.

- [ ] A Sigma rule on Sysmon process events
- [ ] Test it: it should match the renamed copy tool and nothing else
- [ ] When would it have fired, compared with AL-8406?
- [ ] One tuning note


```tool sigma
{"rule": "", "n": 3, "ls": true, "blank": ["rule"], "a": {"rule": "title: Renamed rclone
id: 5a1c7e10-0b8f-4a59-9a3e-2c1f00000402
status: experimental
description: rclone copies files to cloud storage. Running it under another name is how attackers hide data theft.
logsource:
  product: windows
  service: sysmon
detection:
  selection:
    EventID: 1
    OriginalFileName: 'rclone.exe'
  filter:
    Image|endswith: '\rclone.exe'
  condition: selection and not filter
falsepositives:
  - IT tools that bundle rclone under their own name (list them by path and signer)
level: high
tags:
  - attack.exfiltration
  - attack.t1567.002
  - attack.defense_evasion
  - attack.t1036
"}}
```

?> How many events does your renamed-rclone rule match? :: sha256:4e07408562bedb8b60ce05c1decfe3ad16b72230967de01f640b7e4729b49fce
?> How many minutes before AL-8406 would it have fired? :: sha256:e29c9c180c6279b0b02abd6a1801c7c04082cf486ec027aa13515e4f3884bb6b

## 9. Shift report

Close your shift. Everything open, by ID, with an owner. Everything closed in one line. What the morning should watch. Who you called and when. How many hints you opened.

- [ ] Open items by ID with owners
- [ ] Closed items
- [ ] Watch list including your new rule
- [ ] Calls with times
- [ ] Hints opened

```tool report
{"tpl": "handover", "title": "Shift report: night shift, 11 to 12 Nov", "text": "", "n": 5, "blank": ["text"], "a": {"text": "# Shift report: night shift, 11 to 12 Nov

## Still open

- INC-1112 (AL-8401, AL-8403, AL-8404, AL-8406, AL-8408): client files copied from acc-lt03 to cloud storage through a remote access tool. Escalated at 01:18 UTC. Next: client isolates the laptop; morning analyst lists exactly which files were copied and helps the client decide who must be told. Owner: morning shift lead.
- AL-8412: unknown device android-7f3a on the staff Wi-Fi. Needs more information: ask the client's office manager whether a staff member connected a new phone today. Owner: morning analyst, by 03:00 UTC.

## Closed this shift

- AL-8402: benign, a.nguyen's own inbox rule for tax-office letters, made in Outlook from the office.
- AL-8405: benign, Windows Update restarts during the patch push CHG-0417.
- AL-8407: benign, typing mistakes with Caps Lock on, then a good logon from the same desk.
- AL-8409: benign, the monthly archive job CHG-0412.
- AL-8410: benign, service installed during the patch window CHG-0418.

## Watch for

- Any host contacting ledgerpro-support.example, relay.remotehelper.example or downloads.toolmirror.example.
```
